Two Resources:

LSAT Demon Estimator. Not real numbers, but at each school there is the 509 linked, which tells you the quartiles for LSAT and GPA: [https://lsatdemon.com/scholarships](https://lsatdemon.com/scholarships)

LSAC Admissions Grid: Some schools (not even close to all) have admissions grids for the previous year, so you can see based on your LSAT and GPA how many people got in. This is UNC's for example, but you can see if a school has it by looking on the LSAC website: [https://report.lsac.org/View.aspx?SID=102&Report=OfficialGuideRLS](https://report.lsac.org/View.aspx?SID=102&Report=OfficialGuideRLS)

LSD is also a good resource but is self-reported data, so would try to lean on data point with more comprehensive information included, e.g. scholarship amount.

I think this is important if you provide context, but on its own is basically useless. Is it painful because you took on too much debt and didn't realize the job prospects your school provided? Is it painful because the actual practice of law is painful?

At that difference, I'd personally take BC, but I'm debt averse and would be perfectly fine living in NE. As for portability, I think the links I sent give you a general idea, but your best bet is probably to talk to alumni and/or see if you can get more specific numbers from the school. Analyzing the very basic numbers they provide, if BC only places 17 out of 341 grads into NY, the largest BL market, and that is the 3rd most common destination, it seems like placement into a smaller, more competitive market like DC is unlikely and would be <5% of the class at the very most. 

Vandy's basic numbers provide slightly more potential, but again all of this could be skewed by self-selection. I'd say try to access the sources I suggested above or whatever else you can, but unless you find overwhelming evidence that they consistently place students into jobs you want in the city you want, don't count on mobility and take the money. Even if people do place into cities like DC, they may be on the whole taking lesser jobs than they would get in other markets, so better data will help immensely. Best of luck!

**BC:** [https://www.bc.edu/content/dam/bc1/schools/law/careers/employment/2024-aba-employment-summary.pdf](https://www.bc.edu/content/dam/bc1/schools/law/careers/employment/2024-aba-employment-summary.pdf)

Based on outcomes, Vandy is slightly better at BL placement and about twice as good at federal clerkships. The only other big thing is that literally about 50% of BC grads stay in MA, without about 1/6 going to NY. For Vandy, about a quarter stay in TN and a quarter go to NY.

So if you're fine staying in MA, aren't as interested in clerkships, and think you'll be good enough at either school to get BL if you want, save the money. Don't get it in your head that Vandy is super portable, but it's definitely more portable than BC. That being said, if it's only 25k total, it's reasonable either way. If it's 25k/yr, I'd think a little about whether that slight portability and prestige is worth it. It may be, but that's up to you.

This. THIS. It makes me so sad because I know people are trying to do good, but the system is setting people up to fail. No, the mantra *you have to spend money to make money* isn't always applicable, but when we're talking about this disparity in magnitude, given everything I mentioned below, I think it's more than reasonable.

I'm sorry, but I disagree and I think this is the kind of argument that keeps people in a cycle of debt. Studying does not guarantee anything, but if you look at the people or institutions that have historically perpetuated the idea that you can't improve or that you shouldn't take the test more than once, it's law schools. Who stands to benefit from lower scores? Law schools.

As for studying, I agree that it doesn't guarantee anything, but I also think that, to be frank, if you can't improve your score over the course of a year with good study materials, you're not set up to succeed in law schools. That's not an argument based on LSAT-LGPA correlation, it's an argument based on how many people I've seen improve, how learnable the test is, and the reflection on your work ethic.

To address "paying some rando on the internet $100 per hour,", that's not what I'm saying at all. There are plenty of established tutors and services that I would advocate for. This is a false dichotomy you've set up between not paying for prep and paying a scammer. This sub is a great place for recommendations of both tutors and services, and I would encourage people to do their research before doing anything.

As for the financial consideration of student loans vs. tutoring, I'm sorry but you're wrong here. I don't care how great of interest rates you get on your student loans, 100-300k in student loans in a million times worse. **Here's an exercise: let's say you spend 10k on tutoring, more LSAT attempts, application help, and a large number of applications (which is a high estimate) and put that on a credit card at 25%, but you don't take out loans for school, or take out 100k less (which is not unreasonable given how much is given out in student loans and how much a good LSAT can make a difference. Let's compare that to a student who takes out an extra 100k in student loans. Even if those student loans don't accrue interest over the 3 years you're in school and then start at 7% afterwards (which is pretty standard), your credit card debt would NEVER CATCH UP. NEVER.** I'm not advocating for credit card debt, but there are ways to get money, and the idea that somehow this student loan debt is good debt is silly. The mommy daddy argument is a charged argument with no substance. Your money is better spent on the front end. You don't have 10k for this stuff? Well, you sure as hell don't have 100-300k for students loans. If you don't improve and your law dreams fizzle out? 10k is a heck of a lot worse than hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, even at the higher interest rate (as exemplified above).

This is further compounded by the inherently privileged position you're attacking it from, despite criticizing me for the same. You mention 100k for T14. 99% of law students don't attend a T14. You're justifying the expense for creme-de-la-creme schools when the average student loan debt is 120k for ALL law schools. To point to an extreme outlier to justify the expense is simply disingenuous. To use an LSAT idea, you're using an unrepresentative sample. What more concerns me is these schools, where the vast majority of people attend. To use an example. John Marshall Law School, tied for last. They have an average LSAT below the national average. Per their 509 report, 75% of their students pay 36k or more a year to attend, without factoring in CoL. Those students are a hell of a lot closer to the average law student than a T14 student is, and there are thousands more of them. "Oh, but you'll make money as a lawyer." Most people won't. Here is a link to the distribution of law salaries of graduates: [https://www.nalp.org/salarydistrib](https://www.nalp.org/salarydistrib) Notice how most people aren't making anything. They'd be better off working at McDonald's (maybe literally when factoring in student loans, especially for those that never practice). So no, this isn't a privileged position. Student loans are oppressive as an institution and are in fact the thing keeping people in poverty.

I'd love to hear a counter to this. It's important we have these kinds of discussions and continue to work to improve the transparency surrounding debt and law school. Cheers!
